title: 'Dynamic entry' to home with 11 tactical officers needed, officer tells inquest
article: A "dynamic entry" was required to carry out the search of a London computer programmer's home to ensure he didn't destroy evidence and because of his troubled past, a London police officer testified at the opening day of an inquest.

Sgt. Jeremy Elliott, a former member of the emergency response unit, was the first witness to provide evidence at the coroner's inquest into the death of Samuel Maloney, 35, who was fatally shot during a police raid on his Old South home on Dec. 23, 2016.

According to an agreed statement of facts, police launched a criminal investigation after racist and misogynistic material was posted on the website of the Hyland Cinema, where Maloney worked as a programmer and systems administrator. An offensive email also was sent to the theatre's subscriber list signed "Sam Maloney AKA God."
Police obtained a warrant to search Maloney's home at 56 Duchess Ave. in London and arrest him for mischief to data and unauthorized use of a computer system.

Elliott crafted the operational plan to conduct a dynamic entry - a tactical police manoeuvre that involves quickly forcing their way into a location and securing it - at the home where Maloney lived with his common-law wife and two young children.

Maloney had a history of violence and erratic behaviour, was known to keep weapons in his home and had frequent run-ins with police in the months leading up to the pre-dawn raid, according to the operational plan presented to tactical officers before they went to the home.

"At the time, under the circumstances, we also believed the dynamic entry was our safest method, not only for ourselves, but for everyone inside," Elliott said Tuesday under questioning from inquest co-counsel Elizabeth Brown.
Elliott detailed the operational plan that included the driving route, how police would enter the house, where paramedics would be staged, each officer's role, contingency plans and other details.

Brown asked Elliot whether the charges against Maloney, both property offences, were considered when making the plan that involved 11 tactical officers forcing their way into the home where children were inside.

"Any plan should be a result of the totality of the circumstances, so the charges are one circumstance," Elliott said. "The location, the people you're dealing with, their history, access to firearms, previous dealings with police, time of day, all of these things are circumstances that have to be taken into consideration when making up the plan."
Inquest co-counsel Roger Shallow briefly described what happened after police entered Maloney's house and encountered him and his common-law wife, Melissa Facciolo, inside an office.

Maloney fired a crossbow at an officer, prompting the officer to return fire before taking cover in another room. Facciolo fled to a rear bedroom where officers were holed up with the couple's children. Police tried to negotiate with Maloney before he ran toward the rear bedroom with a hatchet over his head and was fatally shot.
Shallow told the jury the synopsis doesn't "reflect the entirety of the evidence" they'll hear during the inquest that's expected to last 15 days.

"It's equally important to consider the factors that led to the decision to put those officers in that position in the first place. In other words, to execute that warrant dynamically in the first place," he said.
The inquest is mandatory under the Ontario Coroner's Act and will hear the facts surrounding Maloney's death. A five-person jury will make non-binding recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
Facciolo and one of Maloney's brothers read statements Tuesday, describing Maloney as a talented but troubled man who had big dreams and loved his family.

"As we begin this inquest, I ask you to remember that Sam's story is not just one of tragedy nor uniqueness, but a loss of an exceptional mind, a misunderstood man who, despite his struggle, had love, compassion and humanity within him," Facciolo said of the man she'd known since they were children.

"He was someone's smiling little boy once, a father, a brother, a partner and a friend. I believe he deserved the chance to be helped and that we owe it to him and his family to fully understand the circumstances that led to his violent and untimely death and to appreciate the person he truly was."
Peter Maloney described his sibling as a caring older brother who excelled in computing and mathematics at a young age.

"Sam saw what others missed or just could not see and could work out a problem until arriving at a coding solution not yet seen," he said. "He was a pioneer ahead of his time and mastered skills that were in their infancy."
But Maloney's mental health struggles as an adult led to anti-social behaviours including distrust of authority and paranoia, his brother said.
The inquest resumes Wednesday with more evidence from Elliott.
